title: SlotDrop: Group Reflection
subtitle: ITMGT 45.03, Group 1 | 27 November 2026
pages: SlotDrop started in October with a familiar idea: help businesses sell capacity that would otherwise go unused. Building it made that idea much less abstract. An empty workshop seat is only sellable before a particular session and its preparation cutoff. A customer also needs to know that the seat will still be there while they finish booking. GC2 gave us a working discovery-to-confirmation flow and a score of 105/100. For the Final, we chose to improve the reservation between selection and confirmation, because that is where our promise to the customer has to become something the system can actually enforce.

Our USP is a server-enforced, ten-minute hold on workshop seats. It gives a customer time to finish while reducing the seats available to other customers; an expired hold releases that availability. A spreadsheet could record an interested customer, but someone would still have to coordinate competing requests and enforce the deadline. SlotDrop applies the same rule across those requests. On screen, the feature belongs in Selection and Checkout as a reservation status and countdown, then in the saved booking as its hold reference. The clearest demonstration is an active hold that completes and an expired hold that refuses with a reason.

The server already creates, reads and releases persisted holds. It sets expiry to the earlier of ten minutes or the studio's booking cutoff, so a reservation cannot outlast the session's own rules. In our controlled example, holding two of four seats leaves two available to other customers. Once the hold expires, the server can return four without depending on an open browser or a running countdown. The countdown is therefore an explanation of the server's decision, rather than the mechanism that protects the seats. The remaining frontend handoff must make that distinction visible to someone using the app for the first time.

Janelle's new booking integration closes another part of that promise. A quote can recognize the customer's matching hold without treating their own reserved seats as unavailable. Confirming converts that hold and saves the booking in one database transaction. The seats move from held to booked and are counted once. An expired or mismatched hold is refused; an identical retry returns the original receipt, including after the original reservation window has passed. We checked this against the existing price and retry rules because adding a reservation should not undo the safeguards that earned us good GC2 feedback.

The one GC2 comment we prioritized was the first-visit delay of about 22 seconds. We chose it because it affects whether anyone reaches the prototype at all. It also affects the first click of the live demo, where the audience has no reason to know that a slow page is a sleeping host rather than a broken application. GC2 had already recognized the session lock, stale-price refusal, identical retry behavior and financial model. Improving first access addressed an observed weakness while preserving those working parts. We wanted our next change to improve what a user experiences, rather than add another feature that is difficult to reach.

Our response was a health route, a workflow configured to ping it every ten minutes, a warm-up before presenting and a local fallback. We checked actual scheduled executions and a logged HTTP 200 response instead of assuming that writing the schedule meant it was running. That evidence still does not guarantee uninterrupted responsiveness, so we will check recent execution and the first load before deciding where to start the defense. The local version follows the same application rules and retains its data between runs. This gave us a more practical definition of readiness: choose a working starting point and know how to recover.

The V2 tinker checks also caught two problems that were easy to miss when following only the happy path. After a successful booking, Back could restore Checkout still saying "Saving" with its actions disabled. We changed successful navigation to replace the completed form with the saved receipt, so Back returns to a usable Selection page. Typing an invalid quantity could also leave session details saying "Loading" after validation had already stopped the request. The error now names Quantity, preserves the loaded session and keeps Continue disabled. In both cases, the database could be correct while the customer was left unsure what had happened.

A more consequential bug involved an Owner edit. If the studio moved its booking cutoff earlier, an existing hold could retain its original, later expiry. The system was then making two different promises about the same seat. We changed the cutoff edit so affected holds are shortened in the same transaction. Moving the deadline later does not restart the customer's ten-minute window. This changed how we checked edits: showing the new value on screen was not enough. We also had to ask what happened to records created under the previous value and whether their promises still made sense.

Another integration issue appeared when Home reused grouped workshop cards. Their date-option styles had been scoped to Browse, so dates, prices and cutoffs ran together on Home. We added scoped Home styles and checked phone and desktop widths. The shared renderer was working, but it depended on layout rules that had not travelled with it. That was a useful reminder to test a reused component in the page where it will actually appear. Passing the right data into a function did not establish that the result was readable or that its recovery state was usable.

The reservation work made our team handoffs very concrete. Fran's persisted hold endpoints, Janelle's quote and conversion, Kat's Selection and Kaitlyn's Checkout have to agree on one session, quantity, hold ID and expiry. Kirsten's shared states must reflect that same availability; Chonel's Home handoff is now integrated and tested against it. An early boundary check returned "Unsupported quote field: holdId", identifying exactly where the pieces were not yet connected. The new backend now accepts it; the visible countdown and frontend handoff remain the next integration step. We will only describe the full USP as complete when a customer can see it act and finish the same journey.

Our November 16 outside-group iPhone test had already shown someone following the GC2 booking flow and saving a one-seat Bumi & Ashe booking for PHP 2,880. A separate readback matched the receipt in Owner. We are retaining that evidence while checking changed paths directly, because an earlier successful test cannot prove a later build. The V2 browser checks covered Back, receipt Refresh, empty selection, manually entered invalid quantities, repeated Confirm, direct Detail links and an unmatched search. We also checked phone widths and browser errors. Repeated Confirm produced one saved booking, which mattered more than simply observing that the button became disabled.

We are claiming the Owner analytics bonus. Its five figures come from saved records: booking count, platform fee revenue, average booking value, the top-selling workshop and the number of nearly full sessions. This makes the Owner screen useful beyond confirming a save. It helps the studio judge which workshops are filling and lets us check whether the platform is earning the commission our model assumes.

Compared with October, we now ask more precise questions about whether a system works. We check which record was saved, whether availability changed once, what a second customer sees and how the first customer recovers after a refusal. We also distinguish a failed request from an uncertain result: if the booking may already exist, recovery must reuse its request identity. That approach carries into how we use AI assistance. Generated code still has to be traced through our own routes and rules, tested against the actual contract and disclosed. A test result is useful only for the behavior and build it actually checked.

Our next business step would be a small pilot with one consenting studio. The sourced studio references and simulated bookings establish neither a partnership nor demand. We would collect actual released capacity, attendance, preparation cutoffs and support costs, then compare SlotDrop bookings with the studio's direct sales. At the demo prices, two standard seats pay the studio PHP 4,860 after commission, while two buddy seats pay PHP 4,617. If those customers would have booked anyway, the studio loses PHP 243. The discount therefore needs to add attendance or improve overall contribution. Calculating a lower price correctly does not establish that offering it is a good decision.

Our four-week scenario sells 32 of 64 released seats across 28 bookings, generating PHP 8,532 in platform fees. After assumed support costs of PHP 1,400 and outreach and operations of PHP 6,000, SlotDrop keeps PHP 1,132 before founder time, taxes, future payment costs and refunds. At that sales mix, modeled break-even is about 27 seats; the downside can still lose money. The next pilot must test those assumptions rather than treat them as achieved sales. Our decision is to retain a 10% commission for a one-studio pilot, use 27 of 64 released seats as the modeled break-even checkpoint, and expand only when actual costs leave both SlotDrop and the studio with a positive contribution.
implementationStatus: Hold-aware quote and atomic backend conversion verified; visible countdown and Selection/Checkout handoff remain teammate integration. Refresh those two implementation-status passages only when the full on-screen flow passes.

bonusClaim: Owner analytics; five server-computed figures verified.
